---
title: "D10 Use of AI agents in development"
---

## What was delegated

This platform was built with AI coding agents, and so was this documentation. The
developer set the requirements, approved each plan, took the design decisions and reviewed the results; an
agent wrote almost all of the code, the tests and the first draft of most prose, and nearly
every commit in the repository's history carries an agent co-author line. A validator
should read everything here knowing that.

{{< yt S1-c1 >}}

What was delegated, across the build:

| Work | What the agent did | What stayed with the developer |
|---|---|---|
| The five modules and the portal | wrote the code, training scripts, reports and tests, stage by stage | the gates, the leakage deny-list, the choice of methods, which results to accept |
| The loan workbench (`app/v2`) | executed a written plan task by task; a separate agent reviewed each task and the whole | the plan, the rule that every number comes from a module function, the decision to ship |
| This documentation's facts layer | wrote the code that computes every fact through the modules, the generated tables, the lint and the `verify.py` check | the list of facts, the values each had to reproduce, the rule that no number is typed by hand |
| This documentation's prose | drafted the chapters from a written brief per section | every finding, every classification and tier, and the final wording |

## How every output is checked

An agent's output is treated like a junior analyst's: plausible, fast, and not evidence
until checked. The checks are the same ones this documentation describes for the models,
and none of them relies on the agent's own account of what it did.

- **Gates** (D9). A model an agent trains must pass a committed gate, and `verify.py`
  recomputes the metric with its own copy of the gate. An agent that relaxed a gate to get
  a model through would fail the checkpoint.
- **`python verify.py`**. Every gate and every fact is recomputed from the committed data
  and models, or read from the committed artifact named under its source, on every run
  (the stress refits under `--full`). An agent's report that "all checks pass" is replaced by running the checks.
- **The lint**. No number can be typed into these pages by hand; every one is a named fact
  computed through the modules. An agent paraphrasing a number from memory — the most
  common way a model document drifts from its model — fails the build.
- **Human review of numbers against the source**. Where a number appears in teaching
  material outside the lint's reach, the developer re-executes the code that produced it and
  reads the result against the claim.
- **Independent review**. Larger pieces of agent work were reviewed by a separate agent
  instance given only the requirements and the diff, then by the developer.

## A mistake caught late: the leakage probe

Session 1 teaches leakage with a probe: add a column that would not exist at decision time
and watch the AUC rise. For weeks, every artifact that described the probe — the lab
sheet, the slides, the run of show and the facilitator's timer — said the AUC would reach
about 1.0.

The code all of them shipped leaked a different column: the generator's *true PD*, not the
default outcome itself. Leaking the true PD does not give a near-perfect model. It gives a
plausible improvement, the kind that passes review. Only leaking the outcome reaches 1.0.

Each piece looked right on its own. The code ran. The prose was fluent and internally
consistent. Nothing failed, because nothing compared the two. The error was caught only
when the developer executed the notebook cell before the session and read its output
against the sentence on the slide.

The fix made the mistake the lesson. The probe became a three-rung ladder — honest
features, then the leaked true PD, then the leaked outcome — and the teaching point moved to
the middle rung: a leak that looks like a good model, ships, and then performs no better
than the honest model once the true PD it depended on no longer exists.

What it changed in how agents are used here:

- a number in prose must come from executed code, never from a description of the code;
- the check compares the claim with the output — checking each separately is not enough;
- this documentation's facts layer and lint exist so that the comparison is automatic.

## What the regulators expect of AI

OSFI's E-23 (effective 2027) defines a model to include AI and machine-learning methods,
and expects governance to mature with them: explainability requirements set by the model's
purpose, autonomy and customer impact (Principle 3.3), explainability assessed in
independent review (Principle 3.4), and monitoring that handles AI-specific challenges
such as autonomous decision-making (Principle 3.6). The PRA's SS1/23 asks firms to
identify and manage the risks of AI in modelling techniques, and to weigh a model's
interpretability, explainability and potential for bias when setting its tier
(Principle 1.3).

Neither document addresses AI used to *build* a model, as opposed to AI that *is* the
model. None of the four models here, nor the pricing tool, is itself an agent: the
scorecard is a logistic regression, the adjudication, early-warning and line-increase
models are gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM), and pricing is a deterministic calculation. This chapter applies the same
principle to the tools that built them: an agent's contribution is documented, its output
is independently checked, and responsibility for the result stays with a named person.
